key_insight: The paper introduces Tensor Similarity — a weight-space metric that determines when two tensor-based network parts implement the same computation by being invariant to weight-space symmetries, enabling comparison beyond mere empirical behavior. This provides a principled, basis-independent test for mechanistic equivalence.
problem_solved: Existing similarity measures either rely on empirical behavior (and fail out-of-distribution) or compare raw parameters (and break under weight-space symmetries); the paper provides a symmetry-invariant, weight-based way to verify whether two subnetworks implement the same mechanism.
method: Define a tensor-based similarity metric that is invariant to common weight-space symmetries (e.g., permutation, sign/orthogonal changes) so comparisons reflect computation, not basis choice.
Operationalize the metric via tensor factorizations and alignment procedures to compute canonical or symmetry-quotiented representations of components.
Validate the metric on synthetic and real model components, showing it detects mechanistic equivalence where behaviour-based or naive parameter metrics fail, especially OOD.
impact: Provides practitioners and interpretability researchers a robust tool to verify and track computations across models, checkpoints, or architectures—improving model understanding, component reuse, and trustworthy mechanistic claims. It reduces false negatives/positives caused by basis changes or distribution shifts.
visual_elements: Schematic: two subnetworks with different bases but identical computation, connected by a tensor-similarity arrow indicating invariant matching.
Heatmap/matrix of similarity scores comparing pairs of components (tensor similarity vs baseline metrics) to show improved alignment.
Flowchart: compute tensor canonicalization → alignment under symmetry group → similarity score — annotated with inputs/outputs.
Benchmark chart: detection accuracy of mechanistic equivalence across OOD tests for tensor similarity and competing methods.
paper_title: When Are Two Networks the Same? Tensor Similarity for Mechanistic Interpretability
paper_authors: ML Nissen Gonzalez, Melwina Albuquerque, Laurence Wroe, Jacob Meyer Cohen, Logan Riggs Smith
